1	\begin{abstract}
2	Test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, yet for named entity recognition (NER), where outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, a persistent gap separates quality estimation from sample selection.
3	We ask whether entity-level agreement signals can bridge this gap.
4	Across nine method categories spanning diagnostic probes, selection/construction strategies, and learning-based approaches, we find that no entity-level agreement signal reliably improves selection.
5	Quality estimation signals correlate with oracle F1 ($\rho$ up to 0.47, AUROC up to 0.82) yet no signal selects better than greedy decoding.
6	The failure is systematic: a four-stage diagnostic cascade (quality estimation $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ log-probability compression) localizes where and how selection breaks down, with cross-task validation on RE and SQL parsing (87.2\% output degeneracy).
7	A hidden-state linear probe achieves entity-level discrimination (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] $0.63$\textendash$0.88$, dataset-dependent) from a single forward pass, consistently exceeding prompt-based self-evaluation (AUROC 0.51) but matching multi-sample agreement ($0.87$) only on the simplest task.
8	These negative results delineate where self-consistency (SC) does succeed for IE: through paths that bypass entity-level agreement.
9	Log-probability selection improves F1 by $+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.021$, selection family $k{=}21$), entity-level construction via weighted voting gains $+1.02$\textendash$1.40$\,pp, and cross-model ensembles add $+0.42$\,pp on Few-NERD.
10	Each exploits sequence-level or cross-model signals rather than entity-level self-verification.
11	Strict majority vote fails to improve F1 on any dataset ($\Delta$ from $-2.7$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); a degeneracy decomposition confirms gain vanishes once output degeneracy exceeds 70\%.

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, yet for named entity recognition (NER), where outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, a persistent gap separates quality estimation from sample selection.
We ask whether entity-level agreement signals can bridge this gap.
Across nine method categories spanning diagnostic probes, selection/construction strategies, and learning-based approaches, we find that no entity-level agreement signal reliably improves selection.
Quality estimation signals correlate with oracle F1 ($\rho$ up to 0.47, AUROC up to 0.82) yet no signal selects better than greedy decoding.
The failure is systematic: a four-stage diagnostic cascade (quality estimation $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ log-probability compression) localizes where and how selection breaks down, with cross-task validation on RE and SQL parsing (87.2\% output degeneracy).
A hidden-state linear probe achieves entity-level discrimination (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] $0.63$\textendash$0.88$, dataset-dependent) from a single forward pass, consistently exceeding prompt-based self-evaluation (AUROC 0.51) but matching multi-sample agreement ($0.87$) only on the simplest task.
These negative results delineate where self-consistency (SC) does succeed for IE: through paths that bypass entity-level agreement.
Log-probability selection improves F1 by $+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.021$, selection family $k{=}21$), entity-level construction via weighted voting gains $+1.02$\textendash$1.40$\,pp, and cross-model ensembles add $+0.42$\,pp on Few-NERD.
Each exploits sequence-level or cross-model signals rather than entity-level self-verification.
Strict majority vote fails to improve F1 on any dataset ($\Delta$ from $-2.7$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); a degeneracy decomposition confirms gain vanishes once output degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
\end{abstract}

866	Table~\ref{tab:within_rho} reports median within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ across datasets, computed over non-degenerate instances (those with ${\geq}2$ distinct F1 values across $N{=}8$ samples).
867	Few-NERD exhibits substantially stronger alignment ($\rho{=}0.667$) than SciERC ($\rho{=}0.262$), directly explaining why LP selection succeeds only on Few-NERD.
868	CoNLL alignment is moderate ($\rho{\approx}0.51$), but the valid-instance fraction is low (38\% for Qwen, 11\% for LLaMA) because degeneracy eliminates most headroom before alignment can operate.
869	LP-quality alignment is the primary predictor of selection direction; degeneracy constrains headroom but does not independently predict whether LP selection gains materialize (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

1559	\paragraph{Temperature controls degeneracy and LP spread.}
1560	Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy} reports instance degeneracy (constant F1, gold-filtered) and median within-instance LP range across four temperatures on SciERC.

1562	Temperature thus provides a direct lever for practitioners to shift the degeneracy regime.

1621	\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
1622	The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
